after.storage: Keep raw filling and waiting uncooked dumplings refrigerated at 40°F /4°C or below, bringing out small wrapping batches. Use clean utensils and plates for cooked dumplings. When making ahead, freeze uncooked dumplings promptly in a single layer on a lined tray, then transfer once firm to an airtight freezer container. Assembly does not restart the storage clock of the raw meat or seafood. Refrigerate cooked leftovers in shallow containers within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F /32°C; use within 3–4 days and reheat to 165°F /74°C throughout. Store soup broth separately and bring reheated soup to a rolling boil.

## Chef's Note

Cantonese wonton soup features delicate pork wontons in clear, aromatic broth. Stirring the pork filling vigorously in one direction until it becomes sticky and tacky is a traditional technique that ensures the filling stays cohesive during boiling.

**The Broth:** This recipe relies on [Cantonese Wonton Broth](/mise/recipes/cantonese-wonton-broth). You can use high-quality chicken stock infused with ginger/scallion in a pinch. Broth and wrappers must be ready before starting; making either from scratch takes additional time. Allow longer if your pot requires several wonton batches.

## Directions

1.  **The Filling:** In a large bowl, whisk pork, scallions, ginger, soy, wine, and broth in one direction until sticky.
2.  **Assemble:** Divide all the filling among the small wrappers, using only as much as each can seal securely; the count may vary with wrapper size. Wet the edges with water. Fold into a rectangle, then pinch the two corners together to form a "hat."
3.  **The Base:** Bring the prepared broth to a boil in a separate saucepan, then keep it hot. In 4 serving bowls, add a few drops of sesame oil and white pepper to taste. Taste the prepared broth before adding salt; the linked broth is already seasoned.
4.  **Boil:** Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Add wontons in uncrowded batches and stir gently to prevent sticking. Begin checking after 3-4 minutes; floating alone is not a doneness test. Check several wontons with a thin-tip thermometer inserted into the center of the filling and continue cooking until they reach 165°F / 74°C. Halve or quarter the bok choy lengthwise, rinse well, and cook it in the hot broth until its stems are tender-crisp; do not rely on 20 seconds for whole heads.
5.  **Bind:** Bring the [Wonton Broth](/mise/recipes/cantonese-wonton-broth) back to a boil if needed. Ladle the hot broth into the serving bowls.
6.  **Serve:** Transfer the wontons and bok choy to the bowls. Garnish with scallions and optional chili oil.

## Chef's Note

This pork wonton soup features delicate pork wontons in clear, aromatic broth. Stirring the pork filling vigorously in one direction until it becomes sticky and tacky is a traditional technique that ensures the filling stays cohesive during boiling.

**The Broth:** This recipe relies on [Cantonese Wonton Broth](/mise/recipes/cantonese-wonton-broth). You can use high-quality chicken stock infused with ginger/scallion in a pinch. Broth and wrappers must be ready before starting; making either from scratch takes additional time. Allow longer if your pot requires several wonton batches.

Keep waiting raw filling and assembled dumplings refrigerated, working with small batches and clean serving utensils.

## Directions

1.  **The Filling:** In a large bowl, whisk pork, scallions, ginger, the filling soy and wine, all the measured binder broth, the filling salt and the filling white pepper in one direction until sticky.
2.  **Assemble:** Divide all the filling among the small wrappers, using only as much as each can seal securely; the count may vary with wrapper size. Wet the edges with water. Fold into a rectangle, then pinch the two corners together to form a "hat."
3.  **The Base:** Bring the prepared broth to a boil in a separate saucepan, then keep it hot. In the listed number of serving bowls, add a few drops of sesame oil and white pepper to taste; keep the broth in the saucepan until the bok choy is cooked and step 5 is ready. Taste the prepared broth before adding salt; the linked broth is already seasoned.
4.  **Boil:** Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Add wontons in uncrowded batches and stir gently to prevent sticking. Begin checking after 3-4 minutes; floating alone is not a doneness test. Check several wontons with a thin-tip thermometer inserted into the center of the filling and continue cooking until they reach 165°F / 74°C. Halve or quarter the bok choy lengthwise, rinse well, and cook it in the hot broth until its stems are tender-crisp; do not rely on 20 seconds for whole heads. Cook uncooked wontons from frozen without thawing, in uncrowded batches in the same separate pot of water; allow longer than for fresh wontons and keep checking several filling centers to 165°F / 74°C and the wrappers for tenderness.
5.  **Bind:** Bring the [Wonton Broth](/mise/recipes/cantonese-wonton-broth) back to a boil if needed. Ladle the hot broth into the serving bowls.
6.  **Serve:** Transfer the wontons and bok choy to the bowls. Garnish with scallions and optional chili oil.
